name: Religious nationalism
summary: Religious nationalism ties national identity and the legitimacy of the state to a particular religion, treating shared faith as the marker and bond of the nation much as language or ethnicity does elsewhere. It is typically a reaction against secular, Western-style nationalism, and seeks a larger public role for religion, religiously informed law and morality, and a privileged position for the majority faith. Its forms differ by tradition, from Hindutva and Pakistani Islamic nationalism to Polish Catholic, Orthodox, Buddhist and religious-Zionist variants, and the sources do not give it a common economic programme.
scope: The family as a whole in the mainstream of its modern forms, not any one movement: the definition and comparative account in Wikipedia's article (drawing on Juergensmeyer, van der Veer and others), Savarkar's Hindutva and Golwalkar's account of the Hindu nation, and Pakistan's 1949 Objectives Resolution as an Islamic example. Excludes theocratic clerical-rule movements as the norm, and treats economic and technology questions as largely unaddressed, so many of those answers are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar
keyFigures.role: Popularised the term Hindutva and defined the Hindu nation by shared fatherland and holy land.

keyFigures.name: M. S. Golwalkar
keyFigures.role: RSS leader who argued that the nation is defined by religion-based culture and that minorities must assimilate or be subordinate.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Economic policy varies by movement; nothing in the ideology's definition addresses wage floors.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The ideology is about identity and religion, and its parties adopt very different economic doctrines, so adherents are split.

public-ownership.rationale: No settled stance on ownership; adherents range from nationalisers to free-marketeers depending on country and party.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Taxation is not a defining issue; positions follow each movement's local coalition rather than the ideology.

unions-good.rationale: Movements are split on labour organisation; the sources give no shared position.

cut-welfare.rationale: Religious charity and communal duty are common themes but movements differ on state welfare, so adherents are genuinely split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Adherents want to protect religion from insult (blasphemy laws) yet resist limits on their own rhetoric, so they are split.

state-harmful.rationale: The ideology treats the state as the vehicle of a religiously defined nation, so abolishing it is rejected.

limit-guns.rationale: Not a defining issue and positions vary by country.

empower-police-military.rationale: Movements defending the religious nation against perceived internal and external threats generally favour strong security forces.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The stricter moral observance that religious nationalism promotes through law makes sex work legalisation strongly opposed.

traditional-family.rationale: Religious nationalist movements, such as Polish Catholic nationalism, defend traditional family and oppose same-sex marriage and abortion.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Religious nationalism is documented as opposing same-sex marriage, for example in Polish Catholic nationalism.

abortion-legal.rationale: Catholic and other religious nationalisms are documented as opposing abortion.

more-religion-public.rationale: Making religion central to public and national life is the defining claim of religious nationalism.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Religious doctrine typically grounds gender in divine or natural order, so adherents reject the constructionist claim.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: National culture, tied to religion, is the object of this ideology; Golwalkar called culture a product of religion.

gradual-change.rationale: Movements often present themselves as restoring tradition yet pursue radical change against secular order; split.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Religion as a national marker leads to wariness of immigration by other faiths, though positions vary by country.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Religious nationalism is a reaction against secular global order and Western-imposed models, so adherents resist more power for the UN.

nation-first.rationale: The nation defined by shared religion is the primary loyalty; adherents generally put it ahead of global cooperation.

open-borders.rationale: Borders define the religiously constituted homeland; Savarkar's Hindutva stresses a bounded fatherland and holy land.

limit-growth.rationale: Economic growth versus environment is outside the sources; religious nationalist parties back growth in practice but nothing is stated.

expand-nuclear.rationale: No ideological position; national-power motives are offset by nothing documented.

revolution-justified.rationale: Some movements (Iran, Taliban) came to power through revolution while others work through electoral politics.

land-value-tax.rationale: A single-tax proposal is unrelated to the religious-national question and nobody in the sources takes it up.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Not a defining issue, though nation-first sentiment inclines slightly toward protection.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial strategy is a matter of national policy rather than doctrine, so adherents are split.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: A class-abolishing, secular-materialist programme is opposed by religious nationalists.

one-party-rule.rationale: Some movements favour a dominant party or clerical rule, while others work within pluralist democracy; Golwalkar dismissed democracy but modern parties compete in elections.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Some religious nationalisms back monarchy (Orthodox, Shinto-era Japan) and others republics.

democracy-best.rationale: Adherents are split: the Objectives Resolution blends popular representation with divine sovereignty, while Golwalkar dismissed democracy as alien.

workers-councils.rationale: Class-based council power conflicts with a religious-national conception of the polity.

natural-rulers.rationale: Religious authority claims differ between movements; split.

political-violence-never.rationale: Some movements (Hamas, Taliban) use violence while mainstream parties do not; most adherents do not accept an absolute ban.

war-builds-character.rationale: No common position; some movements glorify martyrdom while others do not.

separate-church-state.rationale: Religious nationalism is defined against strict secularism; the Objectives Resolution places sovereignty in God.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Many movements want laws to reflect religious law (Islamic principles in the Objectives Resolution), though Hindu and Orthodox nationalists often do so through culture rather than explicit scripture.

private-courts-defense.rationale: The nation-state as vehicle of the religious nation is central, so privatising courts and defense is rejected.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Religion functions as an ethnic marker; Savarkar treated Hindus as one people of common blood and culture.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Religious nationalism rejects class conflict as history's engine; it centres religion and nation. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Some movements claim indigenous status for the religious majority (Hindutva) and others for minorities; split.

civilizational-union.rationale: Many movements envisage religious or civilizational solidarity, such as the Islamic ummah, Orthodox world, and Akhand Bharat, though most work at national level.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Individual self-interest as virtue conflicts with religious duty and communal loyalty.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Golwalkar rejected a nation as a bundle of rights, and religious traditions emphasise duty to community and God.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Some religious traditions sanctify nature but the nationalist movements do not take a common line.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A technology-policy matter with no link to religion or nationhood in the sources.

restore-past-order.rationale: Religious nationalism often presents itself as recovering a more authentic traditional identity against modernity and secularism.

direct-action.rationale: Movements use both mass mobilisation and elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: Movements differ on whether violent or coercive means fit their goals; nothing settled in the sources.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not compatible with traditional social order.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Marxist exploitation theory is rejected by religious nationalism.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Class dictatorship is opposed by religious nationalists, who define the nation by religion. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Marxist theory is rejected, though anti-Western feeling is common.

harm-principle.rationale: Religious nationalists want law to enforce morality and religious observance, beyond preventing harm.

state-as-business.rationale: The state as sacred or communal vehicle is incompatible with a customer-service model.

positive-liberty.rationale: The idea that freedom needs material means is a liberal-socialist debate absent from the sources.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not a core claim, though Savarkar spoke of common blood.

organic-representation.rationale: Representation through families and communities appears in clerical-corporatist strands but not the mainstream, so split.

national-rebirth.rationale: The movements frame themselves as reaction to modernity and secular decline, seeking national renewal on religious lines.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Savarkar imagined a pan-Hindu world and Akhand Bharat, but many movements are defensive.

bound-labor.rationale: Not part of any modern religious nationalism.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Religious Zionism is one documented example (s1), but Islamic, Hindu and Christian religious nationalisms each centre their own homeland and many Islamic ones reject Israel, so across the family the answer is 0 at low confidence.

revive-national-language.rationale: Hebrew revival and Sanskritisation are examples, but not a general doctrine.

economic-freedom.rationale: The link between political and economic freedom is a liberal thesis the sources do not touch.

national-self-determination.rationale: Religious nationalism claims a state for its nation, as in Pakistan's two-nation theory (s1, s5), but Hindutva denies separate nationhood to Muslims and Kashmiris, so it does not extend the claim to every nation.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Religious nationalism makes faith central to public life and is a reaction against secular rationalism. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Workfare is a policy dispute outside the sources; adherents differ by party.

class-collaboration.rationale: Communal unity across classes is a theme; Savarkar stressed one people across castes.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Inherited institutions are valued as carriers of national religious identity, so sacrificing them is rejected.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Documented in movements promoting traditional family and gender roles, as Polish Catholic nationalism.

ban-interest.rationale: Islamic strands favour it while other traditions do not.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not a defining religious-nationalist demand, though communal separation appears in some.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Religious nationalism treats the state as an expression of the religious nation, not of a ruling class.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Golwalkar's minorities choice of adopting the national culture or subordination reflects assimilationist demand.

elite-replacement.rationale: Not a core claim; some religious nationalists voice demographic fears.

national-mission.rationale: Some movements claim universal religious missions, others only national.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Religious-nationalist adherents defend traditional roles rather than call them systemic advantage.

night-watchman-state.rationale: A state with religious and cultural functions is incompatible.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Communal endogamy appears in some movements; Savarkar allowed converts to intermarry.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Religious traditions assert equal worth of persons but religious nationalism often privileges the majority's rights, as in Golwalkar's subordinate minorities.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Hindutva supports a uniform civil code, while Islamic and Jewish religious nationalists favour religious personal law; adherents split by tradition.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Hindutva-linked states pass conversion bans and many religious nationalisms restrict proselytism, though positions vary.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Religious instruction in schools is a normal demand; Polish and other nationalisms support it.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Objectives Resolution sets power as a trust from God exercised through elected representatives, mixing consent and divine limits.

population-transfer.rationale: Golwalkar's text demanded subordination of minorities and other movements pursued transfers, but mainstream adherents do not state it; split.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not a position held; many movements accept force for defence of faith and nation.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social Darwinist claims are not made in the sources; religious doctrine often stresses harmony instead.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: This republican theory is absent from the sources.

separated-powers.rationale: The Objectives Resolution provides an independent judiciary and federalism, but the ideology does not require it.

vanguard-party.rationale: A Leninist party model is rejected by a religious-national outlook that rests on shared faith rather than class consciousness.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Labour law is not a doctrinal matter here and parties differ.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Shared religion is treated as the glue of national unity, so religious plurality is seen as weakening it; Golwalkar demanded minorities merge into the national culture.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Offices tied to religious and national legitimacy are not distributed by lot.

party-controls-media.rationale: Some movements in power control media while others compete in plural systems.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline is organisational; some cadre movements like the RSS-BJP family are disciplined but sources give no doctrine.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Religious nationalism is a reaction against secular supranational orders, so pooling sovereignty is disfavoured.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Depends on tradition; Orthodox and Catholic nationalists favour bishops while others have no bishops.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Revolutionary defeatism is opposed to loyalty to the national-religious state.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Religious nationalists commonly seek to restrict art that offends religion or morals, including blasphemy rules.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Term limits are not a doctrinal concern and adherents vary by country.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Alliance policy varies, with some movements seeking alliances with co-religionist states and others none.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A communist-style demand that has no place in religious-nationalism.

people-in-arms.rationale: Militias exist in some movements while others rely on professional armies.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Hindutva's Akhand Bharat and similar claims reflect a desire to reunite a nation across borders.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Religious nationalists typically put their own religious civilization above others, as in Golwalkar's assimilation demands.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Religious nationalists want religion reflected in schooling; but Hindu and others vary, so moderate.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Public morality enforcement through law is a standard religious-nationalist demand.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Savarkar's definition rests on ancestry and shared blood, and religion marks belonging.

minority-language-support.rationale: Golwalkar demanded minorities adopt the national language and culture.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Religious nationalism defends the majority religion's primacy rather than exemptions for minorities.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Conformity to religious and national custom is valued.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Pakistan's assembly set objectives, but no general doctrine.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Religious charity favours aid but nation-first sentiment opposes it; split.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Method of electing the head of state is not a doctrinal matter.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Land is sacred in this tradition, as with Savarkar's holy land and religious Zionism's claim to Israel, so territory is seldom traded.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Religious nationalism opposes curbing religious institutions and clergy. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Hindutva supports territorial unity and opposes separatism, and religious nationalisms generally defend the homeland's integrity.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Divine-descent rulers appear in State Shinto but are not general.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Objectives Resolution places power under divine limits and law; rulers are not above them.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy has no link to the doctrine.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Classical mixed-government theory is outside the sources.

leader-cult.rationale: Some movements revere leaders while others avoid it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Islamist strands require it while other traditions do not.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Religious nationalism holds religion and culture drive history, against materialism. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Critics describe Hindutva majoritarianism, and religious nationalists commonly want the majority faith's will to prevail.

moral-incentives.rationale: Religious duty overlaps but not a stated policy.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Marxist-Leninist foco theory is not a doctrine here, though some armed movements fit.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Orthodox and monarchist strands defend titles while others do not; the sources show no shared view.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Hindutva and similar movements push national-civilizational history in school curricula.

patriotic-education.rationale: Teaching national and religious loyalty in schools is a standard demand.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Pakistan's resolution guaranteed rights subject to law and morality; no firm doctrine.

minority-veto.rationale: Majority and national unity prevail over minority consent in Golwalkar's account.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Objectives Resolution places Pakistan's legislature under divine limits, while others accept parliamentary sovereignty, so split.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Hindu and Buddhist strands say yes, other strands less; split.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Dharmic traditions are vegetarian-leaning and Abrahamic ones accept animal use, so adherents split.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Religious nationalism is political engagement by definition. No cited source discusses this statement directly.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: World-systems theory is absent from the sources.

party-own-road.rationale: This question is about communist parties and does not apply here.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Akhand Bharat and similar claims aim at recovering lost homeland territory.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Heritage preservation is core to national-religious identity.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Movements define their identity against imposed Western secular models, presenting an authentic tradition.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Army political roles vary, with Turkey and Pakistan giving the military a guardian role but others not.

filial-duty.rationale: Traditional family and duty are core to religious conservatism.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Some movements back co-religionist insurgents; not defining.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Religious nationalists hold duty to community and law.

religious-nation.rationale: Religion as the marker of national belonging is the core claim of the ideology, as with Savarkar's fatherland-and-holy-land definition of a Hindu.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Golwalkar and Hindutva writers treat minority communities as of divided loyalty to the nation, which shades into suspicion of hidden disloyalty; not every movement states it.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Religion, which this ideology puts at the centre of public life, treats marriage as sacred and legally regulated, so adherents oppose abolishing its legal standing.

public-access-to-information.rationale: The ideology does not address it, and its parties are split between transparency rhetoric and secrecy in office.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: The sources give no economic programme, and strands diverge on regional fiscal arrangements.

religion-illusion.rationale: Religious nationalism treats religion as the lasting basis of national identity and a reaction against secular modernity, so it rejects the idea that religion fades.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purification occurs in some forms (e.g. Sanskritised Hindi in Hindutva circles) but not across the family, so adherents are split.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: The movements are not economic doctrines and span market and welfare camps, with some framing religious nationalism as an alternative to both.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Savarkar's definition of a Hindu rests on India as both fatherland and holy land, and religious-Zionist and other variants likewise ground the nation's claim in sacred history.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The duty is specific to Islamic variants; Hindu, Orthodox or Buddhist forms have no equivalent, so the family as a whole is split.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Polish Catholic and Hindutva forms often say yes, while Pakistani and other Muslim nationalisms say no, so adherents are split.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: The Objectives Resolution places sovereignty in Allah as a delegated trust, and religious nationalism generally grounds the state's legitimacy in the faith, though Hindutva and Buddhist forms put it less theologically.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Religious nationalism seeks a larger public role for religion, so barring religious dress in state institutions runs against its core aims.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Foreign alignment is not defined by the ideology; movements have both allied with blocs and stressed independence.

reification.rationale: A Marxist-derived analysis of capitalism is not part of the doctrine and adherents are split on economics.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Religious nationalism is not an economic doctrine and its movements span welfare-minded and market-minded camps.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Savarkar and Golwalkar present the Hindu nation as continuous from ancient times, as the sources on Hindutva describe.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Honouring those who die for the nation and religion follows from fusing the nation with a sacred cause, as the Wikipedia overview describes.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: The comparative account in the sources shows these movements frame national politics as a sacred or religious struggle.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Its core claim is that national life rests on religion, with a public role for faith and morality.

racial-group-interests.rationale: The group is defined by faith, though Hindutva texts use race language; adherents split.

racial-pride.rationale: Pride in the faith-nation is central, but race as such is not; adherents split.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: No common doctrine on use of force; movements differ.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Religious nationalism makes shared faith, not language, the marker of the nation, as in Savarkar's fatherland-and-holy-land definition, so it resists language alone defining a nation.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Environmental policy is not part of the ideology and varies by movement; nothing in the sources addresses taxing pollution.

open-diplomacy.rationale: No documented position; movements in government have used both public and confidential diplomacy, so adherents are not clearly divided either way.

collective-bargaining.rationale: The ideology is not an economic doctrine and its movements differ on unions.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Views on global economic reform vary by movement and the sources are silent.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: The ideology prescribes religious and cultural order, not an economic blueprint.

sacred-nation.rationale: Savarkar defines the nation through fatherland and holy land, treating the nation as sacred and enduring.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale turns on whether human nature should be redesigned, and the statement now asks only whether a shared human nature is the basis of rights.

reviewHistory.rationale: Religious conservative nationalists such as Polish Catholics oppose redesigning human nature on moral grounds, though sources only cover abortion and same-sex marriage.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale turns on whether human nature should be redesigned, and the statement now asks only whether a shared human nature is the basis of rights.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Positions differ by tradition, with religious law on inheritance in some forms and statutory equality in others.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Religious nationalism has no economic or environmental programme in the sources, and adherents split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The ideology gives the majority faith a privileged public position, as in the Objectives Resolution and Hindutva's Hindu nation, and so rejects treating all interpretations or faiths as equal before the state.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Economic policy is not part of the definition and varies by movement.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Religious nationalism treats religion as the bond of the nation and a source of morality, so it rejects the claim that religion is a major cause of women's oppression.

national-church-status.rationale: The sources define it by a privileged public position for the majority faith, as in the Objectives Resolution's Islamic principles and Hindu rashtra.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Hindutva and similar strands stress territorial and cultural unity of one national religion and treat minorities as guests or subordinate to it.

simple-living.rationale: Not part of the sources' account of the ideology; traditions differ, and some stress piety and modesty.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Savarkar defines a Hindu through a fatherland that is also a holy land, and other religious nationalisms likewise sacralise the national territory.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Religious nationalism makes the majority faith the basis of the nation and public life, as in the Objectives Resolution's Islamic principles, so politics organised outside religion is rejected.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Religious nationalism is not an economic doctrine and its movements split on distribution; the sources are silent.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: No common position on international finance can be drawn from the sources; adherents differ by tradition.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: The sources give no common view on where value comes from; adherents differ by tradition.

material-over-identity.rationale: Shared faith is the bond of the nation, so religious and cultural identity comes before class interests.

police-more-powers.rationale: Movements defending the religious nation against perceived internal and external threats generally favour strong security forces. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Religious charity and communal duty are common themes but movements differ on state welfare, so adherents are genuinely split. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: The national community should be defined by a shared religion.
missingStatements.rationale: Religion as the marker of national belonging is the core claim of the ideology, as with Savarkar's fatherland-and-holy-land definition of a Hindu.

missingStatements.text: Sovereignty belongs to God rather than to the people.
missingStatements.rationale: The Objectives Resolution begins by placing sovereignty over the universe in Allah, with state power a delegated trust.

missingStatements.text: Religious minorities should be required to adopt the national culture or accept a subordinate position.
missingStatements.rationale: Golwalkar gave minorities this choice, a position critics document as assimilation or exclusion; not every religious nationalism states it.
missingStatements.declined: Covered by assimilate-immigrants and population-transfer; not every religious nationalism states it.

missingStatements.text: Blasphemy or insult to the majority religion should be a criminal offence.
missingStatements.rationale: Protecting the national religion's symbols through law follows from treating it as the basis of the nation; the sources describe it indirectly, so the answer is moderate.
missingStatements.declined: Indirectly sourced and covered by laws-from-scripture and apostasy-punishable.

notes: Strands differ sharply: Hindutva is ethno-cultural and often distances itself from scripture-based law, Islamic nationalisms want law based on Islamic principles, and Catholic and Orthodox forms centre on moral issues. The audit rests mostly on encyclopedic summaries, because Savarkar's and the Objectives Resolution's own texts could not be opened. Economic and technology answers are largely low-confidence neutrals, which may trigger the inclusion check.
